title: The great imams' age
hookLine: Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad teach in this age, and Ja'far al-Sadiq before them

cards: A teacher in Medina sits with a circle of students. In the circle, the biographies say, are two men who will each become the name of a whole way of practicing Islam.
The teacher is Ja'far al-Sadiq, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, through Husayn. The students, tradition says, include Abu Hanifa of Kufa and Malik of Medina.
One circle, and in it names that Muslims still live by. When someone says they follow a Hanafi or Maliki or Ja'fari school, they're pointing back to rooms like this one.

teach.h: JA'FAR AL-SADIQ, AND THE JA'FARI SCHOOL.
teach.b: Imam here means a leading scholar, someone others follow in prayer and in law. Shia Muslims honor Ja'far al-Sadiq as one of the Imams of the Prophet's family, and a Shia school of law carries his name: Ja'fari.
Then the line of teachers runs on.
Abu Hanifa, in Kufa, taught by discussion, turning cases over with his students, reasoning carefully where no text spoke directly.
Malik, in Medina, gathered the hadith and the living practice of the Prophet's city into a book, the Muwatta.
Al-Shafi'i studied with Malik, the biographies say, then traveled and wrote about how law should be drawn from the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal studied with al-Shafi'i, gathered a great collection of reports, and held to his convictions when the authorities pressured scholars to agree with them. Teacher to student to teacher.
The Sunni schools carry their names: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali.
These schools reach different answers on a range of questions, like where to hold your hands in prayer, or details of fasting and trade.

The imams themselves knew it, and the stories about them are often stories of respect across the differences. One story people tell: a caliph wanted to make Malik's book the one law for every city. Malik said no.

The companions of the Prophet, he said, had spread to many lands, each carrying knowledge, and people should be left with what had reached them. This week walked through stars, light, animals, books and chains of reports.
Today it reaches the teachers whose schools of law Muslims still follow.

how: The Sunni schools of law are the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, and Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school; in daily practice people often learn their school's rulings from a local scholar or imam.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you how to do something right, a parent, a coach, a teacher who explained things patiently, and then think back past them: who taught them, and who taught that person?
Let the chain go back as far as you can imagine it. If you pray, you can remember them and their teachers in your prayer; if not, just hold them in mind with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Madhhab, a school of law: the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali and Ja'fari schools, each carrying forward a teacher's line. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a school of law; literally a way that someone goes.
